title: flumph
description: explain the lore and ecology of the dnd flumph, as well as the publication history

script.draft:
[VISUAL: A glowing, jellyfish-like creature with tentacles drifting through a dark dungeon cavern, soft pastel colors, fantasy art style]

Here's a creature so silly-looking it almost got cut from D&D entirely — and instead became a beloved classic. The flumph: a floating, tentacled disk that squeaks, squirts foul-smelling fluid when frightened, and glows with emotion like a mood ring.

But don't let the goofy exterior fool you. Flumphs are lawful good — genuinely kind, ancient, and deeply wise. They feed by absorbing psychic energy from nearby creatures, which means they instinctively drift toward evil beings. Not to help them. To survive near them. It's a dark little detail hiding inside a very silly monster.

They first appeared in 1982's Fiend Folio — one of the strangest entries in the book. For decades they were a joke. Then fifth edition's Mordenkainen's Tome of Foes gave them a full lore treatment, and fans finally embraced them for real.

The flumph earned it.

script.description: The flumph looks like a cosmic joke — a squeaking, smell-squirting jellyfish floating through dungeon corridors. But this strange little creature has one of the most surprisingly rich lore histories in all of Dungeons & Dragons. From its humble and mocked origins in the 1982 Fiend Folio to a full rehabilitation in 5th edition, the flumph's story is weirder than you'd expect. Watch to find out why this goofy monster might actually be one of D&D's most interesting designs — and subscribe for more monster lore every week.

[VISUAL: A glowing, jellyfish-like creature with tentacles drifting through a dark dungeon cavern, soft pastel colors, fantasy art style]

But don't let the goofy exterior fool you. Flumphs are lawful good — genuinely kind, ancient, and deeply wise. They feed by absorbing psychic energy from nearby creatures, which means they instinctively drift toward evil beings. Not to help them. To survive near them. It's a dark little detail hiding inside a very silly monster.

They first appeared in 1982's Fiend Folio — one of the strangest entries in the book. For decades they were a joke. Then fifth edition's Mordenkainen's Tome of Foes gave them a full lore treatment, and fans finally embraced them for real.

The flumph earned it.
